- paragraph: Some succulents naturally grow leggy over time, and their stretched stems must be cut back to keep them looking good. Others stay in a more compact rosette form and rarely need cutting back.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Succulent varieties like Kalanchoes, Aeoniums, and Echeverias tend to grow long stems as they become mature plants. In this (very) old post, you can see how I had to cut
      - link "my Paddle Plant patch":
        - /url: https://www.joyusgarden.com/my-paddle-plant-patch/
      - text: back because the stems were elongating.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: 2) They’re reaching for the light source.
    - paragraph: If you’ve positioned them against a wall or in a corner, they’ll start reaching toward the light. This produces longer stems and less new growth.
    - paragraph: This can also happen in the winter months when the sunlight is less plentiful.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: 3) The light they’re growing in is too low.
    - paragraph: This may be true for your leggy succulents, especially if growing indoors. Your succulents may not get enough light, and you may notice leggy stems, paler foliage, and smaller leaves.
    - paragraph: This could be due to the lack of sunlight or artificial light. You’ll have to move your succulents to a place with more sun exposure, get a grow light or two, or, if possible, move indoor succulents outdoors.

    - paragraph: You may need to go down to the base of the plant to cut. That was the case with my Paddle Plant patch; I took the stems down to where new offsets had formed at the base.
    - heading "How to Cut Back Succulents With Long Stems" [level=2]:
      - strong: How to Cut Back Succulents With Long Stems
    - paragraph: I use my trusty Felco hand pruners, which I’ve had for ages. If the stems are thin and soft, I prefer my micro pruning snips.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Whatever you use to make the cuts, make sure your
      - link "pruning tool":
        - /url: https://www.joyusgarden.com/clean-and-sharpen-your-pruning-tools/
      - text: is clean and sharp. You want clean cuts, not jagged cuts, and you don’t want infection to set in.
    - paragraph:
      - text: When cutting, I prune straight across the stem above a
      - link "leaf node":
        - /url: https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Anatomical-features-of-nodes-within-current-year-woody-shoots_fig1_340512167
      - text: . I used to take them at an angle but switched to straight across six or seven years ago. It doesn’t seem to make much of a difference.
    - figure "The cuttings I got from pruning that succulent pot. I gave a lot away!":
      - img "Looking down on a box full of assorted succulent cuttings."
      - emphasis: The cuttings I got from pruning that succulent pot. I gave a lot away!
    - heading "What Should You Do with the Cuttings?" [level=2]:
      - strong: What Should You Do with the Cuttings?
    - paragraph: Here’s what you do, whether your succulents grow in the ground or a pot, with those tall, stretched-out succulent stems.
    - paragraph: You can propagate by stem cuttings or by leaf cuttings. Stem cuttings are a much faster method, but if you have the patience, try leaf propagation.
    - paragraph: I got quite a few cuttings, as you can see. I put them in a long, low box, then moved them to my utility room with bright light but no direct sun. They need to be in a well-lit area, but they’ll burn if they get too much sunlight. The amount of light they need while healing over isn’t as great as they would need when growing as plants.
    - paragraph: You’ll want to prep the cuttings. Cut off any curved stems and strip off leaves if needed. You want the stems to be as straight as possible because they’re easier to plant.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The cut end of long-stemmed succulents must heal for at least three to six days. Think of this like you would a wound healing over. Cuttings planted back in the soil too quickly before they have a chance to heal are more subject to
      - link "root rot":
        - /url: https://succulentsbox.com/blogs/blog/root-rot-treatment-for-succulents#:~:text=Trim%20Off%20the%20Roots&text=So%2C%20if%20the%20internal%20part,callous%20for%20a%20couple%20days.
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: I’ve let some succulents heal over for nine months, and they grew just fine. Succulents with fine stems, like
      - link "String Of Pearls":
        - /url: https://www.joyusgarden.com/answering-your-questions-about-string-of-pearls/
      - text: ", only need a couple of days. It’s hot here in Tucson, so I don’t heal succulents over for too long."
    - paragraph: After planting, they’ll have new roots in 1-2 months.
    - paragraph:
      - strong:
        - text: We’ve done many posts and videos on indoor and outdoor succulent care, including propagation. You’ll find them in our
        - link "Succulents Category":
          - /url: https://www.joyusgarden.com/category/succulents/
        - text: .
    - figure "The cuttings after sorting through, giving some away, & prepping them.":
      - img "3 different types of succulent cuttings lined up in a box."
      - emphasis: The cuttings after sorting through, giving some away, & prepping them.
    - heading "How to Plant Your Succulent Cuttings" [level=2]:
      - strong: How to Plant Your Succulent Cuttings
    - heading "1) Remove the top layer of soil (if planting them back in the same pot)." [level=3]:
      - strong: 1) Remove the top layer of soil (if planting them back in the same pot).
    - paragraph: This planting was done two years ago, so the soil mix wasn’t too old or compacted. I removed the top 10″ to make room for a fresh mix. Succulents don’t root too deep, so removing it all wasn’t unnecessary.
    - heading "2) Use a mix formulated for succulents & cacti." [level=3]:
      - strong: 2) Use a mix formulated for succulents & cacti.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Fill or top off the pot with succulent and cactus mix. Succulents need a loose mix that is well aerated so the water can thoroughly drain out and they don’t rot. I use this
      - link "DIY succulent and cactus mix":
        - /url: https://www.joyusgarden.com/succulent-cactus-soil-mix/
      - text: for all my succulent planting, indoors and outdoors.
    - heading "3) Mix in compost." [level=3]:
      - strong: 3) Mix in compost.
    - paragraph: (This is optional, but it’s something I always do). A few handfuls of compost enriches the soil naturally, so the roots are healthy and the plants grow stronger. I mixed some of the fresh blend in with the older soil mix. After the cuttings have rooted in, I’ll apply a 1/2″ to 1″ topping of worm compost. This is my favorite amendment, which I use sparingly because it’s rich.
    - heading "4) Get ready to plant." [level=3]:
      - strong: 4) Get ready to plant.
    - paragraph: With the mix all prepped, it was time to plant. I had a couple of small plants from another pot and started with one of those. I then placed the cuttings in groupings that were pleasing to my eye. You may have to play around with them to get them to go how you want.
    - figure "My new planting. As you can see, I left some space for the cuttings to all grow in. You can pack them in tighter if you’d like. Just know they do grow, especially when the weather’s warm.":
      - img "Looking down on newly planted succulent cuttings in a blue pot growing outdoors."
      - emphasis: My new planting. As you can see, I left some space for the cuttings to all grow in. You can pack them in tighter if you’d like. Just know they do grow, especially when the weather’s warm.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: "Note:"
      - text: How you arrange your cuttings is up to you. Just remember that some grow bigger and taller and will take up more real estate than others. I planted the
      - link "Paddle Plants cuttings":
        - /url: https://www.joyusgarden.com/paddle-plant-propagation/
      - text: on the edge because the leaves are so big, and they produce babies like crazy, taking up more space.

    - heading "How to Maintain the New Succulent Planting" [level=2]:
      - strong: How to Maintain the New Succulent Planting
    - paragraph: Succulents are some of the easiest plants.
    - paragraph: I let the new planting settle in for about five to seven days before watering the mix. I learned this early on, and it’s always worked well for me.
    - paragraph: I’ll water this planting once a week until the weather cools. You don’t want to keep your cuttings as dry as you would an established plant. Remember, the roots are still forming.
    - paragraph: Conversely, don’t give too much water, or the cuttings will rot out. Adjust according to your conditions.
    - paragraph: Keep your cuttings out of any direct hot sun to avoid burn. Bright natural indirect sunlight (moderate to high light exposure) is the sweet spot.
    - paragraph: Now that you know how to get new plants from cuttings, you will have a new succulent collection in no time!
    - heading "Fertilizing/Feeding" [level=3]:
      - strong: Fertilizing/Feeding
    - paragraph: I don’t fertilize cuttings when they’re rooting in because I feel they don’t need it. I do mix in a little compost and worm compost when preparing the potting mix.
    - paragraph: When the cuttings have rooted in and started growing, I start a fertilizing routine.
    - figure "Here’s a newly planted succulent container that is tight & compact. Not for too long!":
      - img "Close up of a beautiful mixed succulent planting with different colors & foliage types."
      - emphasis: Here’s a newly planted succulent container that is tight & compact. Not for too long!
    - paragraph: These steps also work with succulents that have long stalks and are getting too tall. If you have succulent plants growing long stems, simply give them a good haircut. They can take it and will come back stronger than ever. Gotta love these great plants!

- paragraph: Some succulents naturally grow leggy over time, and their stretched stems must be cut back to keep them looking good. Others stay in a more compact rosette form and rarely need cutting back.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Succulent varieties like Kalanchoes, Aeoniums, and Echeverias tend to grow long stems as they become mature plants. In this (very) old post, you can see how I had to cut
      - link "my Paddle Plant patch":
        - /url: https://www.joyusgarden.com/my-paddle-plant-patch/
      - text: back because the stems were elongating.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: 2) They’re reaching for the light source.
    - paragraph: If you’ve positioned them against a wall or in a corner, they’ll start reaching toward the light. This produces longer stems and less new growth.
    - paragraph: This can also happen in the winter months when the sunlight is less plentiful.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: 3) The light they’re growing in is too low.
    - paragraph: This may be true for your leggy succulents, especially if growing indoors. Your succulents may not get enough light, and you may notice leggy stems, paler foliage, and smaller leaves.
    - paragraph: This could be due to the lack of sunlight or artificial light. You’ll have to move your succulents to a place with more sun exposure, get a grow light or two, or, if possible, move indoor succulents outdoors.

    - paragraph: Once a succulent stem gets bare, the leaves won’t grow back on it. You need to cut it back and propagate by stem cuttings or have it rejuvenate from the base (the piece of stem and roots still in the soil).
    - paragraph: How far you cut back depends on how leggy it has gotten and where foliage growth has stopped.

    - paragraph: I use my trusty Felco hand pruners, which I’ve had for ages. If the stems are thin and soft, I prefer my micro pruning snips.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Whatever you use to make the cuts, make sure your
      - link "pruning tool":
        - /url: https://www.joyusgarden.com/clean-and-sharpen-your-pruning-tools/
      - text: is clean and sharp. You want clean cuts, not jagged cuts, and you don’t want infection to set in.
    - paragraph:
      - text: When cutting, I prune straight across the stem above a
      - link "leaf node":
        - /url: https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Anatomical-features-of-nodes-within-current-year-woody-shoots_fig1_340512167
      - text: . I used to take them at an angle but switched to straight across six or seven years ago. It doesn’t seem to make much of a difference.
